subject: sci
title: Cells: Cell Theory, Organelles, Photosynthesis, and Cellular Respiration
objectives: You will state the three parts of the cell theory and use them to judge claims about living things.
You will identify the main organelles and their jobs, and tell plant, animal, and bacterial cells apart.
You will read the equations for photosynthesis and cellular respiration, naming the reactants, the products, and where each process happens.
You will trace energy from sunlight to glucose to ATP and explain how photosynthesis and respiration depend on each other.
You will interpret experiments about photosynthesis and respiration and choose conclusions the data support.

slides.title: Cells: How Living Things Are Built and Powered
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • State the three parts of the cell theory
  • Name the main organelles and their jobs; tell plant, animal, and bacterial cells apart
  • Read the equations for photosynthesis and cellular respiration
  • Trace energy: sunlight → glucose → ATP
  • Interpret experiments about both processes

Plan: Warm-up → 6 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 3 of Science. Life science is about 40 percent of the GED Science test, and cells are where it starts: what they are, what is inside them, and how they get energy. Today is part vocabulary and part reasoning. You will learn a short list of cell parts and two equations, and then you will use them to read experiments the way the GED asks you to.
ask: What do you already know about cells, even one word? (expected answer: anything, such as nucleus, DNA, small, blood cells; use it to connect to today)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Last Week's Data Skills
slides.board:
A student counted the mitochondria in 5 cells: 12, 15, 9, 15, 19.

  1. Find the mean.
  2. Find the median and the mode.
  3. Find the range.
  4. On a slide of 20 cells, 5 are dividing. One cell is picked at random. What is the probability it is dividing?
  5. A seedling grew from 12 cm to 20 cm in 4 days. What was its growth rate?
steps: 1. 12 + 15 + 9 + 15 + 19 = 70; 70 ÷ 5 = 14 mitochondria.
2. In order: 9, 12, 15, 15, 19. Median = 15 (the middle value). Mode = 15 (it appears twice).
3. Range = 19 − 9 = 10.
4. 5 ÷ 20 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.
5. (20 − 12) ÷ 4 = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 cm per day.

notes.say: These five problems review last week's data skills, and they use cell numbers on purpose, because today's experiments will ask for the same math. Give the student about three minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it. If the median or the rate is shaky, fix it now; both show up in today's practice.
ask: What must you do before finding a median? (expected answer: put the values in order)
What does 'per day' tell you to do? (expected answer: divide by the number of days)
notes.watch: Students often take the middle number of the unordered list (9) as the median. Have them rewrite the list in order first. For the rate, some divide 20 by 4 (5 cm per day); remind them that the rate uses the change, 20 − 12 = 8.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: The Cell Theory
slides.board:
1. All living things are made of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
  3. All cells come from cells that already exist.

Built over 200 years: Hooke named cells (1665); Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) showed all living things are made of cells; Virchow added that cells come from cells.

It does not say every cell has a nucleus.

notes.say: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the processes of life: taking in materials, using energy, growing, and reproducing. The cell theory sums up what scientists learned once microscopes let them see cells. Learn the three statements as three short ideas: made of cells, cells are the unit, cells come from cells. The third one matters most on test questions, because it rules out cells forming from nonliving material.
ask: Which part of the cell theory explains how a cut on your skin heals? (expected answer: all cells come from existing cells; skin cells divide to make new ones)
Is a wooden table made of living cells? (expected answer: it was made of cells, wood cells, but those cells are dead now)
notes.watch: Students sometimes add "all cells have a nucleus" to the theory. Bacteria have no nucleus, so that statement is false and is not part of the theory.

slides.title: Worked Example: Test a Claim Against the Cell Theory
slides.board:
Claim: "I boiled some broth, sealed it in a jar, and left it for a month. Bacteria appeared in it. The bacteria must have formed from the broth itself."

Does this claim fit the cell theory? What is a better explanation?
steps: Find the part of the theory that applies: all cells come from cells that already exist.
Compare: the claim says living cells formed from nonliving broth. That contradicts part 3.
Better explanation: a few living bacteria survived the boiling or got in before the jar was sealed. They divided again and again until there were millions.

Conclusion: the claim does not fit the theory. A fair retest would use broth that is truly sterile and sealed so nothing can get in. Experiments like this, done by Louis Pasteur around 1860, found that such broth stays free of microbes.

notes.say: On the GED you may be asked whether a claim or an observation agrees with a scientific theory. The method is the same every time: find the part of the theory that applies, compare it to the claim, and look for a simpler explanation that fits the theory. Here the simpler explanation is contamination, and the fix is a better-controlled test.
ask: What would you expect if the jar were truly sterile and sealed? (expected answer: no bacteria would appear)

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Two Kinds of Cells
slides.board:
ProkaryoticEukaryotic
NucleusNo; DNA floats in the cytoplasmYes; DNA is inside the nucleus
Organelles wrapped in membranesNoYes (mitochondria, ER, Golgi…)
Ribosomes, membrane, cytoplasmYesYes
SizeMuch smallerLarger
ExamplesBacteriaPlants, animals, fungi, protists

Pro = no nucleus. Eu = do.

notes.say: Every cell on Earth falls into one of two groups. Prokaryotic cells, the bacteria, are small and simple: they have DNA, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and a membrane, but no nucleus and no membrane-wrapped organelles. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus that holds the DNA and many organelles inside membranes. The first question to ask about any mystery cell is: does it have a nucleus?
ask: A cell has DNA but no nucleus. Which kind is it? (expected answer: prokaryotic, a bacterium)
Do bacteria have ribosomes? (expected answer: yes; every cell needs ribosomes to make proteins)
notes.watch: Some students think "no nucleus" means "no DNA." Every cell has DNA; in a prokaryote it simply is not enclosed in a nucleus.

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Organelles — The Cell as a Factory
slides.board:
OrganelleJobFactory part
Cell membraneControls what enters and leavesSecurity gate
NucleusHolds DNA; directs the cellMain office
CytoplasmGel that holds the organellesFactory floor
RibosomesBuild proteinsAssembly workers
ER and GolgiProcess, package, shipShipping
MitochondriaRelease energy from glucose as ATPPower plant
ChloroplastsPhotosynthesis: make glucoseSolar panels
VacuoleStores water, food, wastesStorage tank
Cell wallStiff support outside the membraneOuter brick wall

notes.say: An organelle is a small structure inside a cell that does one job. The factory comparison makes the jobs easier to remember: the nucleus is the office with the blueprints, ribosomes are the workers who build proteins, mitochondria are the power plant, and chloroplasts are solar panels. On the GED, the most tested pairs are mitochondria and chloroplasts, because both deal with energy, and cell membrane and cell wall, because both are on the outside.
ask: Which organelle would you expect a lot of in a cell that uses huge amounts of energy? (expected answer: mitochondria)
Which two organelles are both about energy, and how are their jobs different? (expected answer: chloroplasts store light energy in glucose; mitochondria release that energy as ATP)
notes.watch: Students say "mitochondria make energy." Energy cannot be made. Mitochondria release energy stored in glucose and store it in ATP.

slides.title: Worked Example: Classify Three Cells
slides.board:
Cell X: cell wall, ribosomes, a loop of DNA in the cytoplasm, no nucleus.

Cell Y: cell wall, nucleus, chloroplasts, large central vacuole.

Cell Z: nucleus, mitochondria, cell membrane; no cell wall, no chloroplasts.

Classify each as a plant cell, an animal cell, or a bacterium.
steps: Step 1, check the nucleus. X has none, so X is prokaryotic: a bacterium. Its cell wall does not make it a plant; most bacteria have walls.
Step 2, Y has a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic. A cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole point to a plant cell.
Step 3, Z has a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic. No wall and no chloroplasts point to an animal cell.
Routine: nucleus first (prokaryote or eukaryote), then wall and chloroplasts (plant or animal).

notes.say: Watch the order I use. I always check the nucleus first, because that splits bacteria from everything else. Only then do I look for a wall and chloroplasts. If you look at the wall first, Cell X looks like a plant, and that is the trap the GED sets.
ask: Why is Cell X not a plant cell, even though it has a cell wall? (expected answer: it has no nucleus, and every plant cell has one)

slides.title: We Do: Match the Job to the Organelle
slides.board:
1. Cells in the pancreas make large amounts of digestive enzymes, which are proteins. Which organelle would these cells have in large numbers?
  2. A houseplant droops when it runs low on water. Which plant-cell structure has lost water?
  3. A chemical damages a bacterium's cell membrane. What problem will the cell have?
steps: 1. Ribosomes, which build proteins (with plenty of ER and Golgi to package and ship them).
2. The large central vacuole. When it holds less water, it stops pressing out against the cell wall, so the cells go soft and the plant droops.
3. The cell can no longer control what enters and leaves. Materials leak in and out, and the cell will likely die.

notes.say: Let's do these together. For each one, I want you to name the job first, then the organelle that does it. Problem 1: what job is the cell doing a lot of? Making proteins. So which organelle builds proteins? Keep that two-step thinking for every organelle question.
ask: In problem 1, what job does the cell do a lot of? (expected answer: make proteins)
In problem 2, which structure in a plant cell stores water? (expected answer: the large central vacuole)
notes.answer: 1. Ribosomes (supported by ER and Golgi). 2. The large central vacuole lost water, so the cells lost firmness. 3. It cannot control what enters and leaves; it will leak and likely die.
notes.watch: On problem 1, students often say the nucleus because it "controls everything." The nucleus holds the instructions, but the ribosomes do the building.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Photosynthesis
slides.board:
6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen

  • Where: chloroplasts (green pigment chlorophyll captures light)
  • Who: plants, algae, some bacteria
  • In: CO2 from the air, water from the roots, light
  • Out: glucose (food) and O2 (released to the air)
  • Light energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose.

notes.say: Photosynthesis is how plants and algae make their own food. They take carbon dioxide in through tiny pores in their leaves and water up from the roots, and chlorophyll in the chloroplasts captures light energy. That energy is used to build glucose, a sugar, so the light energy ends up stored as chemical energy. Oxygen is released as a by-product, and it is the oxygen we breathe.
ask: What are the reactants, the things that go in? (expected answer: carbon dioxide and water, with light as the energy)
Where does the oxygen we breathe come from? (expected answer: photosynthesis in plants and algae)
notes.watch: The classic reversal: students put oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. Ask, "What do plants give us to breathe?" Oxygen comes out of photosynthesis.

slides.title: Worked Example: Read the Photosynthesis Equation
slides.board:
6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

(a) Name the reactants and products.
(b) Show that each kind of atom is the same on both sides.
(c) How many molecules of oxygen are released for each molecule of glucose made?
steps: (a) Left of the arrow = reactants: carbon dioxide and water (light supplies energy, not atoms). Right = products: glucose and oxygen.
(b) Left: 6CO<sub>2</sub> has 6 C and 6 × 2 = 12 O. 6H<sub>2</sub>O has 6 × 2 = 12 H and 6 O. Total: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O.
Right: C6H12O6 has 6 C, 12 H, 6 O. 6O2 has 12 O. Total: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
(c) The coefficient of O2 is 6 and glucose has a coefficient of 1, so 6 molecules of O2 per glucose.

notes.say: A chemical equation is a recipe: inputs on the left, outputs on the right. The big number in front, the coefficient, tells how many molecules; the small number below, the subscript, tells how many atoms of that element are in one molecule. To count atoms, multiply the coefficient by the subscript. Both sides match, which is the law of conservation of mass you will meet again in chemistry.
ask: In 6H<sub>2</sub>O, how many hydrogen atoms are there? (expected answer: 6 × 2 = 12)
notes.watch: Students add the coefficient and subscript (6 + 2 = 8) instead of multiplying. Write it out: six molecules, each with two H atoms, is 6 × 2.

slides.title: We Do: Counting Oxygen Bubbles
slides.board:
A water plant sits in a test tube under a lamp. A student counts the gas bubbles it gives off in 1 minute, three times at each distance.

LampTrial 1Trial 2Trial 3
Near182124
Far91110

(a) What gas is in the bubbles? (b) Find each mean. (c) What do the results show?
steps: (a) Oxygen, a product of photosynthesis.
(b) Near: (18 + 21 + 24) ÷ 3 = 63 ÷ 3 = 21 bubbles per minute. Far: (9 + 11 + 10) ÷ 3 = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 bubbles per minute.
(c) With less light, the plant made oxygen about half as fast, so less light means a slower rate of photosynthesis.

notes.say: Here the bubbles are our measurement of photosynthesis. Oxygen is a product, so more bubbles per minute means faster photosynthesis. Walk me through the mean for the near lamp first, then the far lamp. Then put the two means side by side and tell me what changed and why.
ask: What is the independent variable? (expected answer: the distance of the lamp, which sets the amount of light)
What is the dependent variable? (expected answer: bubbles per minute)
notes.answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) Near: 21 bubbles per minute; far: 10 bubbles per minute. (c) Less light slowed photosynthesis; the rate dropped to about half.
notes.watch: Some students say the bubbles are carbon dioxide because "plants give off gas." Remind them: plants take in CO2 for photosynthesis and give off O2.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Cellular Respiration and ATP
slides.board:
C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

  • Where: mitochondria. Who: nearly all living things, plants too. When: all the time, day and night.
  • Energy is stored in ATP, the cell's energy currency; some is lost as heat.
  • No oxygen? Fermentation: only 2 ATP per glucose (aerobic: about 30 or more). Yeast → CO2 + alcohol; muscles → lactic acid.

notes.say: Glucose holds energy, but a cell cannot use glucose directly to move or grow. Cellular respiration breaks glucose down with oxygen and moves its energy into ATP, which the cell spends like cash. This happens in the mitochondria of plants and animals alike, every minute of the day. Some energy is always lost as heat, which is part of why your body stays warm. When oxygen runs short, some cells switch to fermentation, which gives far less ATP.
ask: Do plants carry out cellular respiration? (expected answer: yes, all the time, in their mitochondria)
Why do you breathe harder when you run? (expected answer: muscle cells need more oxygen for respiration to make more ATP)
notes.watch: "Plants do photosynthesis, animals do respiration" is the most common misconception in this unit. Ask: "How does a root cell underground, with no light, get its energy?" It respires sugar made in the leaves.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Yeast Balloon Test
slides.board:
Three bottles of warm water each have a balloon stretched over the top.

  • Bottle 1: yeast + sugar
  • Bottle 2: yeast, no sugar
  • Bottle 3: sugar, no yeast

After 30 minutes, only Bottle 1's balloon has inflated noticeably. Explain the results.
steps: Identify the gas: yeast are living cells that break down sugar for energy, and that releases carbon dioxide. The CO2 fills the balloon.
Bottle 2: the yeast are alive but have no sugar to use as fuel, so they release almost no CO<sub>2</sub>.
Bottle 3: no living cells, so nothing breaks down the sugar. This is a control: sugar and water alone do not make gas.

Conclusion: the yeast needed sugar (glucose) as fuel, and CO2 is a product of breaking it down. As oxygen in the bottle runs low, the yeast switch to fermentation, which also releases CO2 (and alcohol). This is why bread dough rises.

notes.say: This is a classic experiment, and the GED likes it because it tests both the equation and experiment design. Notice that each bottle is missing one thing. Comparing Bottle 1 with Bottle 2 shows the sugar matters; comparing Bottle 1 with Bottle 3 shows the yeast matters. That is how scientists use controls to find out what causes a result.
ask: What would happen if you put Bottle 1 in ice water? (expected answer: the balloon would inflate more slowly, because cold slows the yeast's reactions)

slides.title: Your Turn: Cells and Organelles
slides.board:
1. A cell has a nucleus, a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. Is it a plant cell, an animal cell, or a bacterium?
  2. Which organelle controls what enters and leaves the cell?
  3. Most root cells grow underground in the dark. Would you expect them to have chloroplasts, mitochondria, both, or neither?
  4. Which part of the cell theory explains how a cut on your skin heals?
steps: 1. A plant cell (nucleus = eukaryote; wall + chloroplasts + large vacuole = plant).
2. The cell membrane.
3. Mitochondria only. With no light, chloroplasts would be useless; but every living cell needs mitochondria to release energy from glucose.
4. All cells come from cells that already exist. Skin cells near the cut divide to make new ones.

notes.say: Work these alone. You have four minutes. Tell me each answer and how you decided before I reveal it.
notes.answer: 1. Plant cell. 2. Cell membrane. 3. Mitochondria only (most root cells lack chloroplasts). 4. All cells come from existing cells.
notes.watch: On problem 2, listen for "cell wall." The wall gives support; the membrane is the gatekeeper. On problem 3, listen for "neither": root cells still need ATP.

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Two Processes, One Cycle
slides.board:
PhotosynthesisCellular respiration
InCO2 + H2O + lightglucose + O2
Outglucose + O2CO2 + H2O + ATP
WhereChloroplastsMitochondria
WhenOnly in lightAll the time

Matter cycles. Energy flows one way:
sunlight → glucose → ATP → work + heat

notes.say: Put the two equations side by side and they are mirror images: the products of one are the reactants of the other. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms go around and around between plants, animals, and the air. Energy is different. It comes in as sunlight, is stored in glucose, is moved into ATP, and finally leaves as heat. It does not cycle back, which is why life needs a constant supply of sunlight.
ask: In a plant during the day, which processes are happening? (expected answer: both photosynthesis and respiration)
At night? (expected answer: respiration only)
notes.watch: Students say respiration "happens at night" as if it stops during the day. It never stops; at night it is simply the only one of the two that is happening.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Color-Changing Tubes
slides.board:
BTB is a dye that turns from green to yellow as CO2 increases and to blue as CO2 decreases. Four sealed tubes of green BTB water sit in bright light for 24 hours.

TubeContentsColor
1Water snailYellow
2Water plantBlue
3Snail + plantGreen
4BTB water onlyGreen

Explain each tube. Predict Tube 2 in the dark.
steps: Tube 1: the snail respires and releases CO2, so the BTB turns yellow.
Tube 2: in light, the plant's photosynthesis uses CO2 faster than its respiration releases it, so CO2 drops and the BTB turns blue.
Tube 3: the plant removes about as much CO<sub>2</sub> as the snail adds, so the color stays about the same.
Tube 4: the control. It shows the BTB does not change color by itself in light.
Prediction: in the dark the plant cannot photosynthesize but still respires, so CO2 builds up and Tube 2 turns yellow.

notes.say: Indicator experiments are a GED favorite because you have to connect a color to a gas and the gas to a process. My routine: first translate the color into CO<sub>2</sub> up or down, then ask which process adds or removes CO<sub>2</sub>. Respiration adds it; photosynthesis removes it. The plant in Tube 2 is doing both, and the color tells us which one is winning.
ask: Why is Tube 4 needed? (expected answer: it rules out light or time changing the dye by itself)

slides.title: We Do: The Floating Leaf Disks
slides.board:
Spinach leaf disks are soaked in baking soda solution (a source of CO2) until they sink. As they photosynthesize, gas builds up inside and they float. Ten disks go in each cup.

CupLightTime for 5 disks to float
ABright (10 cm)8 min
BDim (50 cm)17 min
CDarkNone floated in 30 min

Name the IV, the DV, the gas, the purpose of Cup C, and one conclusion.
steps: IV: amount of light (set by distance from the lamp). DV: time for 5 of the 10 disks to float.
The gas is oxygen, made by photosynthesis. Baking soda makes sure the disks have plenty of CO2, so CO2 does not limit the results.
Cup C is the control: with no light there is no photosynthesis, which shows the disks do not float for some other reason.
Conclusion: disks in brighter light floated sooner, so the rate of photosynthesis increased with light intensity. Note: a shorter time means a faster rate.

notes.say: This one combines last week's experiment skills with today's biology. Read the setup with me and label it: what changed, what was measured, what stayed the same. Then we decide which process makes the gas. Watch out for the time measurement; a smaller number here is a better result.
ask: Which cup had the fastest photosynthesis? (expected answer: Cup A, because its disks floated in the least time)
Name one controlled variable. (expected answer: the solution, temperature, number of disks, size of disks, the lamp)
notes.answer: IV: light intensity (distance). DV: time for 5 disks to float. Gas: oxygen from photosynthesis. Cup C: control with no light. Conclusion: brighter light gave faster photosynthesis (8 min vs. 17 min).
notes.watch: Students read "17 is bigger than 8" as "Cup B did more photosynthesis." Ask: "Which disks floated first?"

slides.title: Your Turn: The Two Equations
slides.board:
1. Name the two reactants of cellular respiration.
  2. Name the two products of photosynthesis.
  3. How many molecules of CO2 are released when one molecule of glucose is completely broken down by cellular respiration?
  4. A potted plant is kept in a dark closet for two days. Which process does it keep carrying out?
steps: 1. Glucose and oxygen.
2. Glucose and oxygen. (Same two substances: the equations are mirror images.)
3. 6 (the coefficient in front of CO2 is 6).
4. Cellular respiration only. Photosynthesis needs light; respiration never stops.

notes.say: Work these alone in three minutes. Write the two equations at the top of your paper first if that helps. Then tell me each answer.
notes.answer: 1. Glucose and oxygen. 2. Glucose and oxygen. 3. Six. 4. Cellular respiration only.
notes.watch: If the student hesitates on 1 and 2, have them write the IN/OUT columns for each equation. Problem 4 catches anyone who thinks plants only photosynthesize.

slides.title: Your Turn: Read the Data
slides.board:
Oxygen released by a pond plant in 1 hour at different water temperatures:

Temperature (°C)10203040
Oxygen (mL)49136
  1. At which temperature was photosynthesis fastest?
  2. By how many mL did oxygen output change from 10 °C to 30 °C?
  3. Describe the overall pattern in one sentence.
steps: 1. 30 °C (13 mL, the most oxygen).
2. 13 − 4 = 9 mL more.
3. Oxygen output rose from 10 °C to 30 °C, then fell at 40 °C, so warming helps only up to a point.

notes.say: Three minutes. Read the table carefully: the independent variable runs across the top, and the measurement is underneath. When you describe a pattern, describe the whole thing, not just the first part.
notes.answer: 1. 30 °C. 2. An increase of 9 mL. 3. It rose from 10 to 30 °C, then dropped at 40 °C. (Too much heat harms the cell's machinery; students do not need that reason here, but it is a good stretch question.)
notes.watch: On problem 3, many students write "warmer water means more photosynthesis," which ignores the drop at 40 °C. Point at the last column.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: The Mystery Cell
slides.board:
A biologist examines a cell that has a cell wall, ribosomes, a cell membrane, and DNA, but no nucleus.

Which conclusion is best supported?

A. It is a plant cell, because it has a cell wall.
B. It is a prokaryote, because it has no nucleus.
C. It is an animal cell, because it has no chloroplasts.
D. It is not alive, because it has no nucleus.
steps: A is out. Plant cells always have a nucleus. The wall is a trap: most bacteria have cell walls too.
C is out. Animal cells have a nucleus, and animal cells have no cell wall.
D is out. It has DNA, ribosomes, and a membrane. Bacteria are alive without a nucleus; the cell theory does not require one.
B is correct. No nucleus is the defining feature of a prokaryotic cell such as a bacterium.

notes.say: On this kind of question, check the nucleus first, exactly as in the routine. Then go through each choice and find the one fact that rules it out. Notice that every wrong choice uses a real feature of the cell, but draws the wrong conclusion from it.
ask: What single clue settles this question? (expected answer: no nucleus)
notes.answer: B. No nucleus means prokaryote. A ignores the missing nucleus; C ignores the wall and missing nucleus; D wrongly assumes a cell needs a nucleus to be alive.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Best-Supported Conclusion
slides.board:
Three sealed tubes start with green BTB water (yellow = more CO2; blue = less CO2). After 24 hours: Tube 1 (plant, bright light) is blue. Tube 2 (plant, dark) is yellow. Tube 3 (BTB only, bright light) is green.

Which conclusion is best supported?

A. The plant carried out cellular respiration only while it was dark.
B. In light the plant took in more CO2 than it gave off; in the dark it only gave off CO2.
C. The plant carried out photosynthesis in both light and dark.
D. Bright light turned the BTB in Tube 1 blue.
steps: D is out. Tube 3 had bright light and no plant, and it stayed green. Light alone does not change BTB.
C is out. If the plant photosynthesized in the dark, CO2 would not have built up in Tube 2.
A is out. The plant respires in light too; in Tube 1 its photosynthesis simply removed CO2 faster than respiration added it.
B is correct. Blue in light means a net loss of CO2 (photosynthesis winning); yellow in the dark means CO2 was only added (respiration only).

notes.say: This is the same reasoning as the color-changing tubes, now in test form. Translate each color into CO<sub>2</sub> up or down, use the control to rule out the dye changing by itself, and remember that respiration never stops. Choice A is the most tempting because it sounds like the dark tube, so make the student say why it is wrong.
ask: Which tube is the control, and what does it rule out? (expected answer: Tube 3; it rules out light changing the dye)
notes.answer: B. A wrongly says respiration stops in light; C contradicts the yellow dark tube; D is ruled out by the control, Tube 3.

slides.title: Test Strategy: The IN/OUT Box
slides.board:
When a question involves photosynthesis or respiration, draw this on your scratch paper before reading the choices:

INOUTWhere
Photo.CO2, H2O, lightglucose, O2chloroplast
Resp.glucose, O2CO2, H2O, ATPmitochondrion

Wrong choices usually swap IN and OUT or swap the two organelles. Then ask: Is there light?

notes.say: This takes fifteen seconds and protects you from the most common trap on cell-energy questions. Many wrong answers simply reverse a reactant and a product, or put photosynthesis in the mitochondria. With the box in front of you, you check each choice against it. Then ask whether light is present, because that tells you whether photosynthesis is happening at all.
ask: Fill in the box from memory. (expected answer: as shown on the board)

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
1. Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit; cells come from cells.
  2. Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus. Plant cells add a wall, chloroplasts, and a large vacuole.
  3. Photosynthesis (chloroplasts): CO2 + H2O + light → glucose + O2.
  4. Respiration (mitochondria, plants too, all the time): glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O + ATP.
  5. Energy flows: sunlight → glucose → ATP → work + heat.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice (Set A) → Exit Check

notes.say: Let's pull it together. Read each takeaway back to me in your own words. Your next step is the Student Lesson, which walks through every idea again with a check on each screen. Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.
ask: Name three parts a plant cell has that an animal cell does not. (expected answer: cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole)
Why do plants need mitochondria? (expected answer: to release the energy in the glucose they make, as ATP)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Every living thing, from a bacterium to an oak tree to you, is made of cells. On the GED Science test you will see cell diagrams, chemical equations, and experiments about how cells get and use energy. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • State the three parts of the cell theory and use them to judge claims.
  • Tell prokaryotic cells from eukaryotic cells, and plant cells from animal cells.
  • Name the main organelles and their jobs.
  • Read the equations for photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
  • Trace energy from sunlight to glucose to ATP.
  • Interpret experiments about both processes.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Use the hint if you get stuck.

screens.title: The cell theory
screens.html:
A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the processes of life: taking in materials, using energy, growing, and reproducing. Cells were first seen through microscopes in the 1600s. Over the next two hundred years, scientists agreed on three ideas, called the cell theory:

  1. All living things are made of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
  3. All cells come from cells that already exist.

Some living things, like bacteria, are a single cell. Others, like you, are made of trillions of cells working together. Notice what the theory does not say: it does not say every cell has a nucleus, and it does not say all cells look alike.

check.prompt: A student says, "A bacterium is only one cell, so it is too simple to count as a living thing." Which part of the cell theory shows that the student is wrong?
options: All living things are made of one or more cells.
All cells come from cells that already exist.
Every living cell must contain a nucleus and DNA.
Living things are built from organs, not from single cells.
why: This is a true part of the cell theory, but it is about where cells come from. The student's claim is about whether one cell is enough to be alive.
This is not part of the cell theory. Bacteria have DNA but no nucleus, and they are alive.
This is not part of the cell theory. The cell, not the organ, is the basic unit of life, and many living things have no organs at all.
check.hint: Look for the part of the theory that says how many cells a living thing needs.
check.explain: The first part of the cell theory says living things are made of one or more cells. A single cell is enough. A bacterium takes in food, uses energy, grows, and divides, so it is a living thing. "All cells come from existing cells" is also part of the theory, but it is about a different question: where cells come from.

screens.title: Using the cell theory
screens.html:
The GED may describe an observation or a claim and ask whether it fits the cell theory. Use three moves:

  1. Find the part of the theory that applies.
  2. Compare it with the claim. Does the claim agree or disagree?
  3. If it disagrees, look for a simpler explanation that fits the theory.

The third part, cells come from existing cells, is tested most often. It means a new cell is always made when an existing cell divides. Cells do not form from nonliving material such as soil, broth, or dust.

example.prompt: Someone boils broth, seals it in a jar, and a month later finds bacteria in it. They claim the bacteria formed from the broth. Does this fit the cell theory?
steps: The part that applies: all cells come from cells that already exist.
The claim says living cells formed from nonliving broth, so it disagrees with the theory.
Simpler explanation: a few bacteria survived the boiling or got in before sealing, then divided many times.
example.answer: No. The bacteria came from living bacteria that were already in the jar, not from the broth.

check.prompt: Which observation gives the most direct support for the idea that all cells come from cells that already exist?
options: Under a microscope, a yeast cell pinches into two new yeast cells.
Under a microscope, a thin slice of leaf shows thousands of cells.
A muscle cell shortens when it receives a signal from a nerve.
A sample of crushed rock is examined and contains no cells.
why: This supports the first part of the theory (living things are made of cells). It says nothing about where new cells come from.
This shows a cell carrying out a function, which fits the second part of the theory, not the part about where cells come from.
Finding no cells in a rock tells you the rock is not alive. It does not show how new cells are made.
check.hint: Which observation actually shows a new cell being made?
check.explain: Seeing one yeast cell divide into two is direct evidence that new cells are made from an existing cell. The leaf slice supports "living things are made of cells," and the muscle cell supports "the cell is the basic unit of function." Both are true, but neither shows where cells come from.

screens.title: Two kinds of cells
screens.html:
All cells share four things: a cell membrane, cytoplasm (the gel inside), ribosomes, and DNA. Beyond that, cells fall into two groups.

ProkaryoticEukaryotic
NucleusNo; DNA floats in the cytoplasmYes; DNA is inside the nucleus
Organelles inside membranesNoYes
SizeMuch smallerLarger
ExamplesBacteriaPlants, animals, fungi

Memory hook: Pro = no nucleus. Eu = do. When you meet a mystery cell, ask about the nucleus first.

example.prompt: A cell has DNA, ribosomes, a cell membrane, and a cell wall. It has no nucleus. Classify it.
steps: Check the nucleus: there is none.
No nucleus means prokaryotic. The DNA is loose in the cytoplasm.
example.answer: Prokaryotic: a bacterium. The cell wall does not change this; most bacteria have walls.

check.prompt: A cell found in a soil sample is very small. It has DNA in a loop in its cytoplasm, ribosomes, and a cell membrane, but no nucleus. Is it prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Type one word.

mistakes.why: Eukaryotic cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus. This cell's DNA is loose in the cytoplasm and it has no nucleus, so it is prokaryotic.

check.explain: The cell has no nucleus; its DNA floats in the cytoplasm. That is the defining feature of a prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium. Having DNA and ribosomes does not make a cell eukaryotic, because every cell has those.

screens.title: Organelles I: the office and the workers
screens.html:
An organelle is a small structure inside a cell that does one specific job. Picture a cell as a factory.

PartJobFactory part
Cell membraneThin, flexible boundary; controls what enters and leavesSecurity gate
NucleusHolds the DNA; directs the cell's activitiesMain office with the blueprints
CytoplasmGel that fills the cell and holds the organellesFactory floor
RibosomesBuild proteinsAssembly workers
ER and Golgi apparatusProcess, package, and ship proteins and fatsConveyor belts and shipping

A cell that makes lots of protein, such as a cell that makes digestive enzymes, has lots of ribosomes, ER, and Golgi.

check.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

The {{0}} holds the cell's DNA. Proteins are built by the {{1}}. The {{2}} controls what enters and leaves the cell.

options: nucleus
ribosomes
cell membrane
cell wall
why: Ribosomes read instructions to build proteins, but they do not store the DNA. The nucleus holds it.
The cell membrane is the cell's outer boundary. In a eukaryotic cell, DNA is stored in the nucleus.
The cell wall is a stiff outer layer for support. It holds no DNA.

options: nucleus
ribosomes
cell membrane
cell wall
why: The nucleus holds the instructions for proteins, but the ribosomes do the building. Think office versus assembly workers.
The membrane controls traffic in and out; it does not build proteins.
The cell wall gives support; it does not build anything.

options: nucleus
ribosomes
cell membrane
cell wall
why: The nucleus directs the cell, but the gatekeeper at the boundary is the cell membrane.
Ribosomes build proteins inside the cell; they do not control the boundary.
The cell wall is stiff and mainly gives support. Materials pass through it fairly freely; the membrane is what controls entry and exit.

check.hint: Office, assembly workers, security gate: match each to its organelle.
check.explain: The nucleus holds the DNA (the main office with the blueprints). The ribosomes build proteins (the assembly workers). The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves (the security gate). The most common mix-up is the cell wall for the membrane: the wall is a stiff support layer outside the membrane in plants, fungi, and most bacteria.

screens.title: Organelles II: energy and storage
screens.html:
PartJobFactory part
MitochondriaCellular respiration: release the energy in glucose and store it in ATPPower plant
Chloroplasts (plants and algae)Photosynthesis: capture light energy and make glucoseSolar panels
VacuoleStores water, food, and wastesStorage tank
Cell wall (plants, fungi, most bacteria)Stiff layer outside the membrane; support and protectionOuter brick wall

Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the two organelles that handle energy, and they are easy to mix up. Chloroplasts store light energy in glucose. Mitochondria release that energy so the cell can use it. A cell that does a lot of work, such as a muscle cell, has many mitochondria.

check.prompt: A sperm cell swims by whipping its long tail. Many mitochondria are packed into the section of the cell right next to the tail. Which statement best explains this?
options: The mitochondria release energy as ATP that powers the tail's movement.
The mitochondria build the proteins that make up the tail.
The mitochondria carry out photosynthesis to make food for the cell.
The mitochondria store water that keeps the long tail stiff.
why: Proteins are built by ribosomes, not mitochondria. This choice mixes up two organelles.
Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, and animal cells such as sperm have no chloroplasts.
Storing water is the job of vacuoles. Mitochondria release energy.
check.hint: What do mitochondria do, and what does a swimming tail need a lot of?
check.explain: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, releasing the energy in glucose as ATP. Whipping a tail takes a steady supply of energy, so mitochondria are packed right where the energy is used. Building proteins is the ribosomes' job, and photosynthesis happens only in chloroplasts.

screens.title: Plant cells vs. animal cells
screens.html:
Picture a plant cell as a box: a stiff cell wall outside the membrane, a huge water-filled central vacuole in the middle, green chloroplasts, and the nucleus pushed to one side. Picture an animal cell as a soft, roundish bag with only a membrane on the outside.

PartPlantAnimal
Membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomes, ER, GolgiYesYes
MitochondriaYesYes
Cell wallYesNo
ChloroplastsYes, in green partsNo
VacuoleOne large central vacuoleSmall, if any

Common mistake: thinking plants have no mitochondria. Plants make their own food, but they still need mitochondria to release the energy from it.

check.prompt: Looking through a microscope, which two structures would help you decide that a cell is a plant cell and not an animal cell? Select two answers.
options: Chloroplasts
Cell wall
Nucleus
Mitochondria
Cell membrane
Ribosomes
why: Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, so it cannot tell them apart.
Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria. Plants need them to release energy from glucose.
Every cell has a cell membrane, so it cannot tell them apart.
Every cell has ribosomes to build proteins, so they cannot tell plant and animal cells apart.
check.hint: Cross out every structure that both kinds of cells have.
check.explain: Plant cells have three structures animal cells lack: a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. Of the choices, only the cell wall and chloroplasts are on that list. The nucleus, mitochondria, membrane, and ribosomes are found in both kinds of cells. The most common error is choosing mitochondria, as if plants did not need them.

screens.title: Identify any cell: nucleus first
screens.html:
Use the same two-step routine for every mystery cell.

Step 1: Is there a nucleus? No → prokaryote (bacterium). Yes → eukaryote; go to Step 2.

Step 2: Is there a cell wall, chloroplasts, or a large central vacuole? Yes → plant. None of them → animal.

The order matters. Bacteria have cell walls, so if you look at the wall first, a bacterium can look like a plant. Also, not every plant cell is green: cells in roots and onion bulbs get no light and usually have no chloroplasts, but they still have a wall and a large vacuole.

example.prompt: A cell from an onion bulb has a nucleus, a cell wall, and a large central vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Classify it.
steps: Step 1: it has a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic.
Step 2: it has a cell wall and a large central vacuole, so it is a plant cell. The missing chloroplasts make sense: an onion bulb grows underground.
example.answer: A plant cell (one that does not carry out photosynthesis).

check.prompt: Read the lab notes. Click the sentence that proves the cell is NOT a bacterium.
spans: The cell was taken from a sample of pond water.
It is surrounded by a stiff cell wall.
Its DNA is held inside a nucleus.
Ribosomes are scattered through its cytoplasm.
A cell membrane lies just inside the wall.
check.why: Many people click the cell wall sentence, but most bacteria have cell walls too. Only the nucleus rules out a bacterium, because prokaryotes have no nucleus.
check.hint: Which feature do bacteria never have?
check.explain: Bacteria are prokaryotes, and prokaryotes have no nucleus. A cell whose DNA is held inside a nucleus must be eukaryotic. Pond water contains both bacteria and eukaryotes, and bacteria also have walls, ribosomes, and membranes, so none of those sentences settle the question.

screens.title: Photosynthesis: storing the sun's energy
screens.html:
Plants, algae, and some bacteria make their own food by photosynthesis. In plants it happens in the chloroplasts.

6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen

Carbon dioxide enters through tiny pores in the leaves. Water comes up from the roots. The green pigment chlorophyll captures light. The light energy is used to build glucose, a sugar, so the energy ends up stored as chemical energy. Oxygen is released into the air; it is the oxygen you breathe. The plant uses its glucose for energy and as building material, and it can store extra glucose as starch.

check.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

In photosynthesis, the green pigment {{0}} captures light energy. That energy is stored as chemical energy in {{1}}.

options: chlorophyll
ATP
oxygen
the cell wall
why: ATP is an energy-carrying molecule, not a green pigment, and it does not capture light.
Oxygen is a product released by photosynthesis. It does not capture light.
The cell wall gives support. The light-capturing pigment is inside the chloroplasts.

options: glucose
oxygen
water
carbon dioxide
why: Oxygen is released as a by-product. The energy is stored in the sugar that is made.
Water is a reactant that goes in. The energy is stored in the product glucose.
Carbon dioxide is a reactant. Its atoms are built into glucose, and the energy is stored in the glucose.

check.hint: Which product of photosynthesis is food?
check.explain: Chlorophyll, the green pigment in chloroplasts, captures light. The light energy is used to build glucose, so it is stored as chemical energy in the bonds of the sugar. Oxygen is a product too, but it is released as a by-product and does not store the energy.

screens.title: Reading an equation and counting atoms
screens.html:
A chemical equation is a recipe. Reactants (what goes in) are on the left of the arrow; products (what comes out) are on the right.

  • The big number in front is the coefficient: how many molecules.
  • The small lowered number is the subscript: how many atoms of that element in one molecule.
  • Atoms of an element = coefficient × subscript.

In a correct equation, each kind of atom appears in the same number on both sides. Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.

example.prompt: Count the oxygen atoms on each side of 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
steps: Left: 6CO<sub>2</sub> has 6 × 2 = 12 O. 6H<sub>2</sub>O has 6 × 1 = 6 O. Total 12 + 6 = 18.
Right: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> has 6 O. 6O<sub>2</sub> has 6 × 2 = 12 O. Total 6 + 12 = 18.

check.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 6H2O? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: You added 6 + 2. Six molecules each with 2 hydrogen atoms is 6 × 2 = 12.
2 is the number of hydrogen atoms in one water molecule. There are 6 molecules, so multiply: 6 × 2 = 12.
6 is the number of water molecules. Each molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms, so 6 × 2 = 12.

check.hint: Multiply the coefficient by the subscript on H.
check.explain: The coefficient 6 means six water molecules. The subscript 2 means each molecule has two hydrogen atoms. 6 × 2 = 12 hydrogen atoms. A common error is adding (6 + 2 = 8) instead of multiplying.

screens.title: Cellular respiration: releasing the energy
screens.html:
Glucose stores energy, but a cell cannot use glucose directly to move or grow. In cellular respiration, the cell breaks glucose down with oxygen and moves the energy into ATP. This happens in the mitochondria.

C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Respiration happens in nearly all living things, plants included, and it goes on all the time, day and night. The oxygen you breathe in is used in this reaction, and the carbon dioxide you breathe out is one of its products.

check.prompt: Based on the equation for cellular respiration, which substances are used up during the process?
options: Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
Carbon dioxide and oxygen
Glucose and carbon dioxide
why: Carbon dioxide and water are on the right side of the arrow. They are products that respiration makes, not reactants it uses up.
Oxygen is used up, but carbon dioxide is made. You mixed a reactant with a product.
Glucose is used up, but carbon dioxide is a product that is released, the gas you breathe out.
check.hint: "Used up" means reactants. Which side of the arrow are reactants on?
check.explain: Reactants are on the left: C6H12O6 + 6O2, so glucose and oxygen are used up. Carbon dioxide and water are on the right; they are made. If you chose carbon dioxide and water, you named the reactants of photosynthesis, the mirror-image process.

screens.title: ATP and where the energy goes
screens.html:
ATP is the molecule cells use to carry and spend energy. Think of it as the cell's cash: glucose is like money in the bank, and ATP is the bills in your pocket that you can spend right away on moving, growing, and repairing.

Two facts the GED tests:

  • Energy is never created. Mitochondria do not "make" energy. They release energy already stored in glucose and store it in ATP.
  • Some energy is always lost as heat. No energy change is perfect. The heat given off by respiration is part of why your body stays warm.

A full energy path: sunlight → (photosynthesis) → glucose → (respiration) → ATP → work in the cell + heat.

check.prompt: Which statement about energy in cells is correct?
options: Mitochondria release energy stored in glucose and store it in ATP.
Mitochondria create new energy by combining oxygen with water.
Chloroplasts break down glucose to give off light energy.
All of the energy released from glucose ends up stored in ATP.
why: Energy cannot be created. Mitochondria release energy that was already stored in glucose, and oxygen and water are not the fuel.
This runs photosynthesis backward. Chloroplasts use light energy to build glucose; they do not break it down into light.
Some energy is always lost as heat. Not all of it is captured in ATP.
check.hint: Remember two rules: energy is never created, and some is always lost as heat.
check.explain: In cellular respiration, mitochondria release the chemical energy stored in glucose and store part of it in ATP. Energy is not created, so "create new energy" is wrong. Some energy always escapes as heat, so not all of it ends up in ATP.

screens.title: Fermentation: energy without oxygen
screens.html:
When oxygen runs short, some cells can still get a little energy from glucose by fermentation. It releases only 2 ATP per glucose, compared with about 30 or more ATP from respiration that uses oxygen.

WhoProducts of fermentationWhere you see it
YeastCarbon dioxide and alcoholBubbles that make bread dough rise
Hard-working muscle cellsLactic acidMuscles during an all-out sprint

Fermentation explains why you cannot sprint for long: once your muscles depend on it, they get far less ATP per glucose.

check.prompt: When yeast ferment the sugar in bread dough, which gas do they release that makes the dough rise? Type its name or formula.

mistakes.why: Yeast do not release oxygen. Oxygen is released by photosynthesis. Breaking down sugar releases carbon dioxide.
Alcohol is the other product of yeast fermentation, but it is not the gas that makes the bubbles. The gas is carbon dioxide.

check.hint: Look at the table: yeast fermentation makes two products. Which one is a gas?
check.explain: Yeast fermentation produces carbon dioxide and alcohol. The carbon dioxide gas forms bubbles that get trapped in the dough and make it rise. (The alcohol evaporates during baking.)

screens.title: Two processes, one cycle
screens.html:
Put the two equations side by side and they are mirror images: the products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are the reactants of respiration, and the products of respiration (carbon dioxide and water) are the reactants of photosynthesis.

PhotosynthesisCellular respiration
WhereChloroplastsMitochondria
WhoPlants, algae, some bacteriaNearly all living things, plants too
WhenOnly in lightAll the time
EnergyStores light energy in glucoseReleases it as ATP + heat

Matter cycles: the same atoms move back and forth between living things and the air. Energy flows one way: it enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

check.prompt: Sort each statement into the correct category.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting "Happens in plant cells" under photosynthesis only. Plant cells carry out both processes; respiration goes on in their mitochondria all the time.
check.hint: For each statement, check it against both equations and both organelles.
check.explain:
• Photosynthesis only: needs light; releases oxygen.
  • Respiration only: breaks down glucose; takes place in mitochondria.
  • Both: happen in plant cells; involve carbon dioxide (photosynthesis uses it, respiration releases it).

screens.title: Reading indicator experiments
screens.html:
Many GED experiments track a gas to show which process is happening. One tool is bromothymol blue (BTB), a dye that turns yellow when CO2 increases and blue when CO2 decreases.

Routine: (1) Translate the color into CO2 up or down. (2) Respiration adds CO2; photosynthesis removes it. (3) Ask: is there light? Without light, only respiration happens.

A plant in light does both processes. If its tube turns blue, photosynthesis is removing CO2 faster than respiration adds it.

example.prompt: A sealed tube of green BTB holds a water snail and sits in light for a day. It turns yellow. Explain.
steps: Yellow means CO<sub>2</sub> went up.
A snail is an animal: it carries out respiration, which releases CO<sub>2</sub>, and it cannot photosynthesize.
example.answer: The snail's respiration added CO2 to the water, turning the BTB yellow.

check.prompt: A sealed tube of green BTB water holds only a water plant. It is kept in total darkness for 24 hours. What color will the BTB most likely turn?
options: Yellow, because respiration adds CO<sub>2</sub> and nothing removes it
Blue, because the plant removes CO<sub>2</sub> by photosynthesis
Green, because a plant carries out no processes in the dark
Blue, because the plant's respiration uses up the CO<sub>2</sub>
why: Photosynthesis needs light. In total darkness the plant cannot remove CO<sub>2</sub> this way.
Respiration never stops. Even in the dark, the plant's living cells keep releasing CO<sub>2</sub>.
Respiration releases CO<sub>2</sub>; it does not use it up. This reverses the respiration equation.
check.hint: Which of the two processes still happens without light, and does it add or remove CO<sub>2</sub>?
check.explain: In the dark, the plant cannot photosynthesize, but it keeps carrying out cellular respiration, which releases CO2. With nothing removing it, CO2 builds up and the BTB turns yellow. The tempting wrong answer is "green": plants do not shut down in the dark.

screens.title: Measuring the rate of a process
screens.html:
Scientists measure how fast photosynthesis or respiration happens by tracking a product over time:

  • Oxygen bubbles per minute from a water plant (photosynthesis).
  • Time for leaf disks to float as oxygen fills them (photosynthesis).
  • Rise in CO2 in a sealed chamber (respiration).

Repeat each condition in several trials and use the mean. Then read the direction carefully: more bubbles per minute means a faster rate, but a shorter time to float also means a faster rate.

example.prompt: Leaf disks under a bright lamp take 8 minutes to float; under a dim lamp they take 17 minutes. Which had the faster rate of photosynthesis?
steps: The disks float when enough oxygen builds up inside them.
The bright-lamp disks reached that point sooner (8 < 17 minutes).
example.answer: The bright-lamp disks: less time means a faster rate.

check.prompt: A water plant gave off 15, 18, and 24 oxygen bubbles per minute in three trials. What is the mean number of bubbles per minute? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 57 is the sum of the trials. Divide by the number of trials: 57 ÷ 3 = 19.
18 is the middle value (the median), not the mean. Add all three and divide by 3.
You divided by 4, but there are only three trials. 57 ÷ 3 = 19.

check.hint: Add the three trials, then divide by 3.
check.explain: 15 + 18 + 24 = 57. 57 ÷ 3 = 19 bubbles per minute. A mean must fall between the smallest and largest trial, so 57 cannot be right. Here the mean (19) and the median (18) differ because 24 is farther from the middle than 15 is.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Cell theory: all living things are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from existing cells.
  • Prokaryotes (bacteria): no nucleus. Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi): nucleus and membrane-covered organelles.
  • Plant cells only: cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole. Both: membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, mitochondria.
  • Photosynthesis (chloroplasts, in light): 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
  • Cellular respiration (mitochondria, all the time, plants too): C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP.
  • Fermentation: no oxygen, only 2 ATP; yeast make CO2 + alcohol, muscles make lactic acid.
  • Energy flows sunlight → glucose → ATP → work + heat. Matter cycles.

Routine: for a mystery cell, check the nucleus first. For an equation, list IN and OUT before reading the choices.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A.

options: Structure B

why: Structure A is the nucleus (the round body with a smaller circle inside). It holds DNA and directs the cell; it does not capture light.
Structure C is the large central vacuole, which stores water. It does not carry out photosynthesis.

items.hint: Photosynthesis happens in the green organelles that contain chlorophyll. Look for the small bodies with stacked lines inside.
items.explain:
Structure B is a chloroplast: a small oval body with stacks of membranes inside (a second one appears at the upper right). Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are where photosynthesis takes place.

  • A is the nucleus (it holds DNA and contains the smaller nucleolus).
  • C is the large central vacuole (storage of water).
  • D is a mitochondrion, recognizable by its folded inner membrane. It carries out cellular respiration, not photosynthesis. This is the most common wrong choice because both organelles deal with energy.
  • E is the cell wall.

items.prompt: Sort each cell structure into the correct category.
items.why: The most common error is putting the mitochondrion under "Plant cells only" or thinking plants lack it. Plants carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria, just as animals do.
items.hint: Three structures help a plant stand up and make its own food. The others are needed by every eukaryotic cell.
items.explain:
• Plant cells only: cell wall (stiff support), chloroplast (photosynthesis), large central vacuole (stores water and keeps the cell firm).
  • Both: nucleus, cell membrane, and mitochondrion.

The most common error is placing the mitochondrion in "plant cells only" or leaving it out of plants. Plants carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria, just as animals do.

items.prompt: Which statement is one of the main ideas of the cell theory?
options: All cells come from cells that already exist.
All cells contain a nucleus that holds their DNA.
All cells contain chloroplasts for making food.
Cells can form from nonliving material such as soil.
why: Bacteria are cells with no nucleus, so this statement is false and is not part of the cell theory.
Only plant and algae cells have chloroplasts. Animal cells and bacteria do not.
This is exactly the idea the cell theory rejects. New cells come only from existing cells.
items.hint: The cell theory has three parts: what living things are made of, what the basic unit of life is, and where cells come from.
items.explain:
The three parts of the cell theory are: (1) all living things are made of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; (3) all cells come from existing cells.

"All cells contain a nucleus" is false because bacteria have no nucleus. Only plant and algae cells have chloroplasts, and animal cells do not. The idea that cells form from nonliving material is exactly what the third part of the cell theory rejects.

items.prompt:
Complete the description of photosynthesis.

During photosynthesis, a plant takes in {{0}} from the air and water from the soil. Using energy from sunlight, it makes glucose and releases {{1}}. This process takes place in the {{2}}.

options: oxygen
carbon dioxide
nitrogen
glucose
why: Oxygen is what the plant releases in photosynthesis. Taking in oxygen describes cellular respiration.
Air is mostly nitrogen, but nitrogen is not a reactant in the photosynthesis equation.
Glucose is the food the plant makes. It is a product, and it does not come from the air.

options: carbon dioxide
water
oxygen
why: Carbon dioxide is taken in, not released, during photosynthesis. Releasing it describes respiration.
Water is a reactant that comes up from the soil. It is used up, not released.

options: mitochondria
nucleus
chloroplasts
cell wall
why: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, not photosynthesis.
The nucleus holds the DNA. It does not capture light or make glucose.
The cell wall gives support. Photosynthesis happens inside the chloroplasts.

items.hint: Write the equation: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + light → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>. Which side shows what goes in?
items.explain:
The equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

  • Reactant from the air: carbon dioxide.
  • Product released along with glucose: oxygen.
  • Location: chloroplasts.

The common mistake is reversing the gases (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out), which describes cellular respiration, and placing the process in the mitochondria, which is also where respiration happens.

items.prompt: Heart muscle cells contain far more mitochondria than most other cells in the body. Which statement best explains this?
options: Heart muscle cells work constantly and need a steady supply of ATP.
Heart muscle cells need extra mitochondria to carry out photosynthesis.
Mitochondria store the oxygen that the heart pumps around the body.
Mitochondria build the proteins that heart muscle cells use to contract.
why: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, and animal cells have none. Mitochondria carry out respiration.
Mitochondria use oxygen; they do not store it. Oxygen is carried through the body by red blood cells.
Proteins are built by ribosomes. This choice mixes up two organelles.
items.hint: What do mitochondria do, and why would a cell that never stops working need a lot of it?
items.explain:
Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, releasing the energy in glucose as ATP. The heart beats about once every second for a whole lifetime, so its cells need a huge, steady supply of ATP. More mitochondria means more ATP.

Animal cells do not perform photosynthesis. Oxygen is carried by red blood cells, not stored in mitochondria. Proteins are built by ribosomes, so the choice about building proteins confuses two organelles.

items.prompt: Which gas is in the bubbles the student counted, and which process produced it?
options: Oxygen, produced by photosynthesis
Carbon dioxide, produced by photosynthesis
Carbon dioxide, produced by cellular respiration
Oxygen, produced by cellular respiration
why: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide; it does not release it. Its gas product is oxygen.
Respiration does release carbon dioxide, but it does not depend on light. These bubbles stopped completely in the dark.
Cellular respiration uses up oxygen; it does not produce it. Oxygen comes from photosynthesis.
items.hint: The number of bubbles depended on light. Which process needs light, and what gas does it release?
items.explain:
The bubble count rose with more light and dropped to 0 in the dark. Photosynthesis needs light and releases oxygen (6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2).

Cellular respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, and it does not depend on light, so it cannot explain bubbles that disappear in the dark. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide; it does not produce it.

items.prompt: What is the mean number of bubbles per minute when the lamp was 30 cm from the plant? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 42 is the sum of the three trials. Divide by the number of trials: 42 ÷ 3 = 14.
You divided by 5, the number of rows in the table. Only three trials were run at 30 cm, so divide 42 by 3.
16 is the largest single trial at 30 cm, not the mean. Add all three trials and divide by 3.

items.hint: Add the three trials at 30 cm, then divide by the number of trials.
items.explain:
Trials at 30 cm: 14, 12, and 16 bubbles per minute.

14 + 12 + 16 = 42

42 ÷ 3 = 14 bubbles per minute

Check: 14 is between the 20 cm mean (23) and the 40 cm mean (8), which fits the trend. A common error is forgetting to divide (42) or dividing by 5 because the table has five rows.

items.prompt: Why did the student keep the plant at 22 °C during every trial?
options: So that a change in bubble count could be linked to light rather than to warmth
So that temperature would serve as the dependent variable in the experiment
So that the plant would carry out cellular respiration instead of photosynthesis
So that the plant would give off the same number of bubbles at every lamp distance
why: The dependent variable is what is measured: the number of bubbles. Something held constant on purpose is a controlled variable.
Keeping temperature steady does not switch the plant from one process to another. The plant does both whenever there is light.
The student expected the bubble counts to change with light. Holding temperature steady makes sure only light causes the change.
items.hint: A lamp gives off heat as well as light. What could happen to the water if the lamp were moved very close?
items.explain:
The independent variable is the amount of light (lamp distance). A lamp close to the plant would also warm the water, and temperature can affect the rate of photosynthesis. Holding the temperature at 22 °C makes it a controlled variable, so it cannot act as a confounding variable.

The dependent variable is the number of bubbles, not temperature. Keeping temperature constant does not switch the plant from one process to another. And the goal was not identical bubble counts; the student expected the counts to change with light.

items.prompt: Which cell most likely came from the onion bulb?
options: Cell W
Cell X
Cell Y
Cell Z
why: Cell W has no nucleus, so it is a prokaryote: the bacterium. Its cell wall does not make it a plant cell.
Cell X is a plant cell, but it has chloroplasts. An onion bulb grows underground with no light, so its cells lack chloroplasts. Cell X is the green spinach leaf.
Cell Y has a nucleus but no cell wall and no large vacuole, which makes it an animal cell: the human cheek cell.
items.hint: Check the nucleus first. Then decide which plant cell would have no chloroplasts.
items.explain: Use the routine. Nucleus first: Cell W has none, so it is the bacterium. Then wall and vacuole: Cell Y has neither, so it is the animal (cheek) cell. Cells X and Z both have a cell wall and a large central vacuole, so both are plant cells. Cell X has chloroplasts (the green spinach leaf). Cell Z has no chloroplasts, which fits an onion bulb that grows underground in the dark. The tempting wrong answer is Cell X, from the idea that every plant cell is green.

items.prompt: By what percent did the CO2 increase from germinating peas drop when the temperature was lowered from 20 °C to 10 °C? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 45% is the part that was left: 540 ÷ 1,200 = 0.45. The drop is the part that was lost: (1,200 − 540) ÷ 1,200 = 0.55, or 55%.
660 ppm is the amount of the drop, not the percent. Divide the drop by the starting value: 660 ÷ 1,200 = 0.55 = 55%.
You divided by 540, the new value. Percent change uses the starting value, 1,200: 660 ÷ 1,200 = 55%.

items.hint: Percent change = (change ÷ starting value) × 100. The starting value is the 20 °C reading.
items.explain:
Germinating peas: 1,200 ppm at 20 °C and 540 ppm at 10 °C.

Change: 1,200 − 540 = 660 ppm

Percent change: 660 ÷ 1,200 = 0.55 = 55%

Cooling the peas cut their rate of respiration by more than half. A common error is to report 45%, which is the percent that remained, not the percent that was lost.

items.prompt: Which two conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: The rate of oxygen production decreased as the lamp was moved farther from the plant.
Light is needed for the plant to produce oxygen bubbles.
Moving the lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm cut the rate of oxygen production in half.
Light is the only factor that affects the rate of photosynthesis.
The plant stopped all cellular activity when the lamp was off.
The plant would produce more bubbles at 50 cm than at 40 cm.
why: Half of 33 is 16.5, but the 20 cm mean is 23. The rate fell, but not by half.
Only light was tested. Temperature and carbon dioxide were held constant, so the data cannot show that light is the only factor.
Zero bubbles shows only that no oxygen was released. The plant's living cells kept carrying out cellular respiration in the dark.
The trend runs the other way: the farther the lamp, the fewer bubbles. The data predict fewer bubbles at 50 cm, not more.
items.hint: Check each statement against the numbers. Reject any statement about something the student did not test.
items.explain:
Supported:

  • The means fall as distance increases: 33, 23, 14, 8 bubbles per minute.
  • With the lamp off, there were 0 bubbles in all three trials, while every lit trial produced bubbles.

Not supported:

  • Half of 33 is 16.5, but the 20 cm mean is 23, so the rate did not drop by half.
  • Only light was tested; temperature and carbon dioxide were held constant, so the data cannot show that light is the only factor.
  • Zero bubbles means no oxygen was released. The plant's cells were still alive and carrying out cellular respiration in the dark.
  • The trend predicts fewer bubbles at 50 cm, not more.

items.prompt: What was the purpose of Chamber 4, which held glass beads?
options: To show that any rise in CO<sub>2</sub> came from the living peas, not the equipment
To give the peas in the other chambers extra oxygen for cellular respiration
To test whether glass beads respire faster at 20 °C than they do at 10 °C
To serve as a second independent variable to be compared with temperature
why: The beads were sealed in their own chamber, so they could not supply anything to the peas. Glass beads do not produce oxygen.
Glass beads are not alive, so they do not respire at any temperature. They were also tested only at 20 °C.
A control group is a baseline for comparison, not another variable that the experimenter changes.
items.hint: Glass beads are not alive. What would a change in CO<sub>2</sub> in that chamber tell you about the equipment?
items.explain:
Chamber 4 is the control. Glass beads take up the same volume as the peas but are not alive, so they cannot respire. Its CO2 rose by 0 ppm, which shows that the sealed chamber and sensor did not produce or leak in CO2 on their own. So the rises in Chambers 1–3 can be credited to the peas.

The beads are in a separate sealed chamber, so they cannot supply oxygen to the peas. Beads are nonliving, so they do not respire at any temperature, and they were only tested at 20 °C. A control group is a baseline for comparison, not an extra independent variable.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Germinating peas respire faster than dry peas, and cooling them slows respiration.
Dry peas are not alive, because they did not release any carbon dioxide at all.
Germinating peas release carbon dioxide only when the temperature is 20 °C or warmer.
Germinating peas released carbon dioxide because they were carrying out photosynthesis.
why: Dry peas did release CO<sub>2</sub>: 100 ppm, compared with 0 for the glass beads. They were alive and respiring slowly.
Germinating peas released 540 ppm at 10 °C, so they do release CO<sub>2</sub> below 20 °C.
Photosynthesis uses CO<sub>2</sub>; it does not release it. Seeds sealed in a chamber release CO<sub>2</sub> by respiration.
items.hint: Compare Chamber 1 with Chamber 3, then Chamber 1 with Chamber 2. Then check each choice against the exact numbers.
items.explain:
Cellular respiration releases CO2, so a bigger CO2 rise means faster respiration.

  • At 20 °C: germinating peas 1,200 ppm vs. dry peas 100 ppm. 1,200 ÷ 100 = 12, so germinating peas respired about 12 times as fast. Growing seeds need much more energy (ATP).
  • Germinating peas: 1,200 ppm at 20 °C vs. 540 ppm at 10 °C, so cooling slowed respiration.

Dry peas did release CO2 (100 ppm vs. 0 for the beads), so they were alive and respiring slowly. Germinating peas released 540 ppm at 10 °C, so they do not release CO2 only at 20 °C. Photosynthesis uses CO2; it does not release it.

items.prompt: A student wrote this summary of the pea experiment. Click the sentence that makes a claim the data do NOT support.
spans: We measured how much carbon dioxide built up in four sealed chambers over 20 minutes.
The glass beads caused no change in carbon dioxide, so the equipment did not add any carbon dioxide on its own.
At 20 °C, germinating peas released 12 times as much carbon dioxide as dry peas.
Germinating peas released less carbon dioxide at 10 °C than at 20 °C.
This proves that warmer temperatures always speed up cellular respiration in every kind of living thing.
The dry peas released a small amount of carbon dioxide, which suggests they were respiring slowly.
items.why: Some students click the sentence about dry peas because it says "suggests." That sentence is careful and fits the data (100 ppm vs. 0). The unsupported one claims what is true for "every kind of living thing" after testing one kind of seed at two temperatures.
items.hint: Look for a sentence that goes beyond what was tested. How many kinds of organisms and how many temperatures were in this experiment?
items.explain:
The experiment tested only one kind of organism (peas) at only two temperatures (10 °C and 20 °C). It cannot show what happens in "every kind of living thing" or at all temperatures. In fact, very high temperatures damage cells and slow respiration. Words like "proves," "always," and "every" are warning signs of an overgeneralization.

The other sentences match the data: the beads showed 0 ppm; 1,200 ÷ 100 = 12; 540 ppm is less than 1,200 ppm; and dry peas released 100 ppm.

items.prompt: A sealed glass terrarium holds soil, a green plant, and a snail. It sits by a sunny window, and both the plant and the snail stay alive for months. Which statement best explains how they survive with no new air?
options: The plant's photosynthesis supplies O<sub>2</sub> for respiration, and respiration returns CO<sub>2</sub> to the plant.
The plant gives off oxygen day and night, so the snail has plenty to breathe while the plant itself uses none.
The snail and the plant each make their own glucose by photosynthesis, so neither depends on the other at all.
The soil supplies all of the food and the oxygen that the plant and the snail both need to stay alive.
why: Plants release oxygen only in light, and plants use oxygen too, because they carry out respiration all the time.
Snails are animals with no chloroplasts. They cannot photosynthesize; they get glucose by eating plant material.
Soil provides water and minerals, not the oxygen and glucose that cells use. Those come from photosynthesis.
items.hint: Write the IN and OUT of each process. Where does each output go?
items.explain: Photosynthesis (plant, in light): CO2 + H2O + light → glucose + O2. Respiration (snail and plant): glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O + ATP. The products of each process are the reactants of the other, so the gases cycle inside the jar, powered by sunlight coming in. The tempting wrong answer says the plant makes oxygen day and night and uses none; in fact it makes oxygen only in light and uses oxygen all the time.

items.explain:
Structure B is a mitochondrion: an oval body with a folded inner membrane (a second one appears at the lower left). Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, releasing the energy in glucose and storing it in ATP.

  • D is a small vacuole for storage.
  • E is a cluster of ribosomes, which build proteins.

items.prompt: Sort each cell part into the correct category.
items.why: The most common error is putting DNA under "Eukaryotic cells only" because bacteria have no nucleus. Bacteria do have DNA; it simply floats in the cytoplasm instead of being held inside a nucleus.
items.hint: Every cell has a few basic parts. Bacteria lack the nucleus and the organelles wrapped in membranes.
items.explain:
• Bacterial and eukaryotic cells: ribosomes (every cell builds proteins), cell membrane (every cell has a boundary), and DNA (every cell has genetic instructions).
  • Eukaryotic cells only: nucleus, mitochondria, and Golgi apparatus. These are wrapped in membranes, and prokaryotes such as bacteria do not have them.

items.prompt: Biologists discover a new kind of organism living near a hot vent on the deep ocean floor. According to the cell theory, which statement must be true about this organism?
options: It is made of one or more cells.
Each of its cells contains a nucleus.
Its cells contain chloroplasts for making food.
Its first cells formed from minerals in the vent water.
why: The cell theory does not say every cell has a nucleus. Many organisms, such as bacteria, have cells with no nucleus.
Many living things have no chloroplasts, and no light reaches the deep ocean floor. The cell theory says nothing about chloroplasts.
The cell theory says all cells come from existing cells, not from nonliving material such as minerals.
items.hint: The first part of the cell theory applies to every living thing.
items.explain: The cell theory says all living things are made of one or more cells, so a newly discovered organism must be made of cells. It might be a single cell with no nucleus, so "each cell contains a nucleus" is not guaranteed. The idea that cells form from minerals contradicts the third part of the theory: cells come only from existing cells.

Complete the description of cellular respiration.

During cellular respiration, a cell uses glucose and {{0}}. It releases carbon dioxide, water, and energy that is stored in {{1}}. This process takes place in the {{2}}.

carbon dioxide
water
light energy

Water is a product of respiration, not a reactant.
Light energy is needed for photosynthesis. Respiration goes on in the dark.

options: ATP
glucose
chlorophyll
oxygen

Chlorophyll is the green pigment that captures light in photosynthesis. It does not store energy from respiration.
Oxygen is used up in respiration. It does not store the released energy.

options: mitochondria
chloroplasts
ribosomes
