items.hint: Write the equation: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> → 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + energy (ATP). What is on the left with glucose?
items.explain:
The equation is C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP).

  • Reactant with glucose: oxygen.
  • The released energy is stored in ATP.
  • Location: the mitochondria.

The common mistake is mixing in photosynthesis: choosing carbon dioxide or light as a reactant, or chloroplasts as the location.

items.prompt: Cells in the pancreas make and release large amounts of digestive enzymes, which are proteins. Which organelle, the one that directly builds this product, would these cells have in unusually large numbers?
options: Ribosomes, which build proteins
Mitochondria, which release energy as ATP
Vacuoles, which store water and wastes
Chloroplasts, which make glucose from light
why: Mitochondria supply energy for the work, but they do not build proteins. The question asks which organelle builds the product.
Vacuoles store materials. They do not build proteins.
Chloroplasts are found in plant and algae cells, not in human cells, and they make glucose, not proteins.
items.hint: Digestive enzymes are proteins. Which organelle builds proteins?
items.explain: Enzymes are proteins, and proteins are built by ribosomes. A cell that makes huge amounts of protein needs many ribosomes (along with plenty of ER and Golgi to package and ship it). Mitochondria provide energy for the work, which makes them tempting, but they are the power plant, not the assembly line.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why no disks floated in the cup with 0% baking soda?
options: With little CO<sub>2</sub>, the disks made too little oxygen by photosynthesis.
Without baking soda, the disks could not carry out cellular respiration.
The disks in plain water took in too much oxygen from the air to float.
The disks in plain water received no light, so photosynthesis stopped.
why: Cellular respiration uses oxygen and does not make the disks float. The gas that fills the disks is oxygen from photosynthesis, which needs CO<sub>2</sub>.
The disks float when oxygen builds up inside them, so more oxygen would make them float sooner, not keep them down.
Every cup sat 15 cm from the same lamp. Light was a controlled variable; only the baking soda changed.
items.hint: Baking soda supplies one reactant of photosynthesis. Which one, and what product makes the disks float?
items.explain: Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Baking soda supplies CO2. In plain water there was very little CO2, so the disks made very little oxygen, and too little gas built up to float any of them within 30 minutes. Light cannot explain the difference, because every cup had the same lamp at the same distance.

items.prompt: What is the mean time, in minutes, for 5 disks to float in the 0.4% baking soda cup? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 33 is the sum of the three trials. Divide by the number of trials: 33 ÷ 3 = 11.
You divided by 5, the number of rows in the table. Only three trials were run at 0.4%, so divide 33 by 3.
9 is the shortest single trial, not the mean. Add all three trials (11 + 9 + 13 = 33) and divide by 3.

items.hint: Add the three trials for 0.4%, then divide by 3.
items.explain:
Trials at 0.4%: 11, 9, and 13 minutes.

11 + 9 + 13 = 33

33 ÷ 3 = 11 minutes

Check: 11 falls between the 0.2% mean (15) and the 0.8% mean (10), which fits the trend.

items.prompt: Which factor was a controlled variable in this experiment?
options: The distance of each cup from the lamp
The concentration of baking soda in each cup
The time it took for 5 disks to float
The amount of oxygen inside the disks
why: Baking soda concentration is what the student changed on purpose (0% to 0.8%), so it is the independent variable.
The time to float is what the student measured, so it is the dependent variable.
Oxygen inside the disks is what made them float; it changed during the test and was not held the same.
items.hint: A controlled variable is kept the same for every cup.
items.explain: Every cup sat 15 cm from the same lamp, so light was kept the same: a controlled variable. Others include temperature (25 °C), the volume of water (100 mL), and the number of disks (10). The baking soda concentration was changed on purpose (independent variable), and the time to float was measured (dependent variable).

items.prompt: A classmate says Cell J must be an animal cell because it has no chloroplasts. Which evidence from the table best shows that the classmate is wrong?
options: Cell J has a cell wall and a large central vacuole.
Cell J has a nucleus and mitochondria.
Cell J has ribosomes, like all the other cells.
Cell J has no chloroplasts, just like Cell K.
why: Animal cells also have a nucleus and mitochondria, so these features cannot rule out an animal cell.
Every cell in the table has ribosomes, including the animal cell, so ribosomes do not tell cell types apart.
Cell K is the bacterium, and lacking chloroplasts is the very feature the classmate is misreading. This does not argue against the claim.
items.hint: Which structures do plant cells have that animal cells never have?
items.explain: Animal cells never have a cell wall or a large central vacuole. Cell J has both, plus a nucleus, so it is a plant cell. It has no chloroplasts because it is the potato cell, which grows underground and stores food rather than making it. A nucleus and mitochondria are tempting evidence, but animal cells have them too.

items.prompt: By what percent did the CO2 increase for yeast with sugar drop when the temperature was lowered from 35 °C to 20 °C? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 37.5% is the part that was left: 900 ÷ 2,400 = 0.375. The drop is (2,400 − 900) ÷ 2,400 = 0.625, or 62.5%.
1,500 ppm is the size of the drop, not the percent. Divide it by the starting value: 1,500 ÷ 2,400 = 0.625 = 62.5%.
You divided by 900, the new value. Percent change uses the starting value, 2,400: 1,500 ÷ 2,400 = 62.5%.

items.hint: Percent change = (change ÷ starting value) × 100. Start from the 35 °C reading.
items.explain:
Yeast + sugar: 2,400 ppm at 35 °C and 900 ppm at 20 °C.

Change: 2,400 − 900 = 1,500 ppm

Percent change: 1,500 ÷ 2,400 = 0.625 = 62.5%

Cooling the yeast cut their CO2 output by well over half. A common error is to report 37.5%, which is the percent that remained.

items.prompt: Which two conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Raising the baking soda from 0.1% to 0.4% shortened the time for the disks to float.
Without added baking soda, the disks did not make enough oxygen to float within 30 minutes.
Doubling the baking soda from 0.4% to 0.8% cut the time to float in half.
Carbon dioxide is the only factor that limits the rate of photosynthesis.
At 1.6% baking soda, the disks would float in about 5 minutes.
The disks in the 0% cup were dead before the experiment began.
why: The mean went from 11 minutes to 10 minutes. Half of 11 is 5.5, so the time did not drop by half.
Only carbon dioxide was tested. Light and temperature were held constant, so the data cannot show that CO<sub>2</sub> is the only factor.
1.6% was never tested, and the times were leveling off (11 to 10 minutes). The data do not support a prediction that far beyond the tested range.
Nothing in the data shows the disks were dead. Their slow result is explained by the lack of CO<sub>2</sub>, not by the disks being dead.
items.hint: Check each statement against the means. Reject any statement about something the student did not test.
items.explain:
Supported:

  • Mean times fell from 21 minutes (0.1%) to 15 minutes (0.2%) to 11 minutes (0.4%).
  • In plain water, no disks floated within 30 minutes in any trial.

Not supported: from 0.4% to 0.8% the time fell only from 11 to 10 minutes, not by half; only CO2 was tested, so it cannot be called the only factor; 1.6% is outside the tested range and the trend was leveling off; and nothing shows the plain-water disks were dead.

items.prompt: What was the purpose of Flask 4, which held sugar water but no yeast?
options: To show that the CO<sub>2</sub> in the other flasks came from the yeast, not the sugar
To give the yeast in the other flasks extra sugar to break down for energy
To test whether sugar water releases more CO<sub>2</sub> at 35 °C than at 20 °C
To serve as a second independent variable to be compared with temperature
why: Flask 4 was sealed on its own, so nothing in it could reach the yeast in the other flasks.
Sugar water with no yeast was tested only at 35 °C, so it cannot compare temperatures. Its job was to be a baseline.
A control is a baseline for comparison, not another variable that the class changed.
items.hint: Flask 4 has no living cells. What would a change in CO<sub>2</sub> there tell you?
items.explain: Flask 4 is a control. It has the same sugar water and temperature as Flask 1 but no living yeast. Its CO2 rose by 0 ppm, which shows that sugar water does not release CO2 on its own and the sealed flask and sensor did not add any. So the rises in Flasks 1–3 can be credited to the yeast.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Yeast released CO<sub>2</sub> faster at 35 °C than at 20 °C, and far faster with sugar than without it.
Yeast cannot release any carbon dioxide at all unless they are first given sugar to break down.
Sugar water releases carbon dioxide on its own once it is warmed to 35 °C, even without yeast.
The yeast released carbon dioxide because they were carrying out photosynthesis in the flasks.
why: Flask 3 (yeast, no sugar) still rose by 150 ppm. The yeast released some CO<sub>2</sub>, likely by using food stored in their cells.
Flask 4 (sugar water, no yeast, 35 °C) rose by 0 ppm. Sugar water released nothing on its own.
Yeast are fungi with no chloroplasts, and photosynthesis uses CO<sub>2</sub> rather than releasing it.
items.hint: Compare Flask 1 with Flask 2, then Flask 1 with Flask 3. Check each choice against the exact numbers.
items.explain:
Breaking down sugar releases CO2, so a bigger CO2 rise means faster breakdown.

  • Flask 1 vs. Flask 2 (only temperature differs): 2,400 ppm at 35 °C vs. 900 ppm at 20 °C.
  • Flask 1 vs. Flask 3 (only sugar differs): 2,400 ppm vs. 150 ppm, which is 16 times as much.

The tempting wrong answer says yeast release no CO2 without sugar, but Flask 3 shows a small rise (150 ppm).

items.prompt: A student wrote this summary of the yeast experiment. Click the sentence that makes a claim the data do NOT support.
spans: We measured the rise in carbon dioxide in four sealed flasks over 30 minutes.
The flask with sugar water and no yeast showed no change, so the sugar did not release carbon dioxide by itself.
At 35 °C, yeast given sugar released 16 times as much carbon dioxide as yeast given plain water.
Yeast with sugar released less carbon dioxide at 20 °C than at 35 °C.
This proves that yeast break down sugar fastest at exactly 35 °C.
The yeast in plain water released a little carbon dioxide, perhaps by using food stored in their cells.
items.why: Some students click the "16 times" sentence because it sounds too strong, but 2,400 ÷ 150 = 16 exactly. The unsupported sentence claims a best temperature after only two temperatures were tested.
items.hint: Look for a sentence that goes beyond what was tested. How many temperatures did the class try?
items.explain:
The class tested yeast with sugar at only two temperatures, 20 °C and 35 °C. The data show 35 °C was faster than 20 °C, but they cannot show that 35 °C is the fastest of all temperatures; 30 °C or 40 °C were never tried. Words like "proves" and "exactly" are warning signs of an overgeneralization.

The other sentences match the data: Flask 4 rose 0 ppm; 2,400 ÷ 150 = 16; 900 ppm is less than 2,400 ppm; and Flask 3 rose 150 ppm, with "perhaps" marking a careful suggestion.

items.prompt: A sensor in a forest measures the carbon dioxide in the air on a clear summer day. The CO2 level is highest just before sunrise and lowest in the late afternoon. Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: In daylight, photosynthesis removes CO<sub>2</sub> faster than respiration adds it; at night only respiration occurs.
Trees carry out respiration only at night, so they release CO<sub>2</sub> only after dark and none during the day.
Sunlight breaks CO<sub>2</sub> in the air apart during the day, and the gas slowly forms again during the night.
Trees carry out photosynthesis mostly at night, when the air is cool, and they rest during the hot afternoon.
why: Respiration goes on all the time, day and night. During the day, it is simply outpaced by photosynthesis.
Sunlight powers photosynthesis inside leaves; it does not break CO<sub>2</sub> apart in the air. The change is caused by living things.
Photosynthesis needs light, so it cannot happen at night. This reverses the real pattern.
items.hint: Which process removes CO<sub>2</sub>, and when can it happen? Which process adds CO<sub>2</sub>, and when does it stop?
items.explain: During the day, trees carry out both processes, but photosynthesis removes CO2 faster than respiration (of trees, animals, and soil organisms) adds it, so the level falls through the afternoon. At night, photosynthesis stops while respiration continues, so CO2 builds up until sunrise. The tempting wrong answer says respiration happens only at night; it never stops, it just is not outpaced at night.

She collected the oxygen the sprig gave off in 30 minutes and measured its volume. She ran three trials for each color, using a fresh sprig each time.

items.prompt: Which observation gives the most direct support for the idea that all cells come from cells that already exist?
options: One onion root cell is seen splitting into two cells.
A slice of onion root is seen to contain many cells.
An onion root cell is seen taking in water from soil.
An onion skin cell is seen to have a stiff cell wall.
why: This supports the first part of the cell theory, that living things are made of cells. It does not show where new cells come from.
This shows a cell carrying out a function. It does not show a new cell being made.
This describes a cell's structure. It says nothing about where new cells come from.
items.explain: Watching one cell divide into two shows a new cell coming from an existing cell, which is the third part of the cell theory. Seeing many cells in a root supports the first part (living things are made of cells), which is true but is about a different question.

items.prompt: A chemical sprayed on a plant destroys the chlorophyll in its leaf cells. Which process will be most directly affected?
options: Making glucose in the chloroplasts
Releasing energy in the mitochondria
Building proteins on the ribosomes
Storing water in the central vacuole
why: Mitochondria release energy from glucose; they do not use chlorophyll. They would be affected only later, once the plant ran out of glucose.
Ribosomes build proteins and do not use chlorophyll.
The central vacuole stores water. Chlorophyll plays no part in that job.
items.explain: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that captures light energy for photosynthesis. Without it, the plant cannot make glucose. Respiration in the mitochondria would suffer only later, when stored glucose ran out, so it is not the most direct effect.

items.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

A cell that has a cell wall but no nucleus is {{0}}. A cell that has a nucleus, a cell wall, and chloroplasts is {{1}}. Both plant and animal cells release energy from glucose in their {{2}}.

options: a bacterium
a plant cell
an animal cell
why: Plant cells have cell walls, but they always have a nucleus. A cell with no nucleus is a prokaryote.
Animal cells have a nucleus and no cell wall, so this cell does not fit on either count.

options: a bacterium
a plant cell
an animal cell
why: Bacteria have no nucleus and no chloroplasts, so this cell cannot be a bacterium.
Animal cells have no cell wall and no chloroplasts.

options: mitochondria
chloroplasts
cell walls
nuclei
why: Animal cells have no chloroplasts, and chloroplasts store energy in glucose rather than release it.
Cell walls give support. Animal cells do not have them.
The nucleus holds DNA. It does not release energy from glucose.

items.explain: No nucleus means prokaryote, so the first cell is a bacterium (most bacteria have cell walls). A nucleus plus a wall and chloroplasts means a plant cell. Both plants and animals carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria. The trap in the first blank is choosing "plant cell" because of the wall.

items.prompt:
6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

According to the equation, which substances does a plant take in to carry out photosynthesis?
options: Carbon dioxide and water
Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and oxygen
Water and glucose
why: Glucose and oxygen are on the right side of the arrow. They are the products, and they are the reactants of respiration instead.
Carbon dioxide is taken in, but oxygen is released. You mixed a reactant with a product.
Water is taken in, but glucose is the food the plant makes. It is a product.
items.explain: Substances a plant takes in are the reactants, on the left of the arrow: 6CO2 + 6H2O, so carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies energy but is not a substance. Glucose and oxygen are on the right; they are made.

items.prompt: What is the mean volume of oxygen, in mL, given off in green light? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 3.9 is the sum of the three trials. Divide by the number of trials: 3.9 ÷ 3 = 1.3.
1.4 is the value that appears twice (the mode), not the mean. Add all three trials and divide by 3.
You divided by 2. There are three trials, so divide 3.9 by 3.

items.explain:
Green light trials: 1.4, 1.1, and 1.4 mL.

1.4 + 1.1 + 1.4 = 3.9

3.9 ÷ 3 = 1.3 mL

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Photosynthesis was much slower in green light than in red or blue light.
The plant did not carry out any photosynthesis at all in green light.
Blue light is the best color of light for every kind of plant on Earth.
The plant gave off more carbon dioxide in red light than in green light.
why: The plant gave off a mean of 1.3 mL of oxygen in green light. That is a small amount, but not zero, so some photosynthesis happened.
Only one kind of plant was tested. The data cannot support a claim about every plant.
The student measured oxygen, not carbon dioxide. The data say nothing about carbon dioxide given off.
items.explain: Means: red 5.0 mL, blue 5.9 mL, green 1.3 mL of oxygen. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so the plant photosynthesized much more slowly in green light. This fits the background: chlorophyll reflects most green light, so little of it is captured. The tempting wrong answer says no photosynthesis happened in green light, but 1.3 mL is more than zero.

items.prompt: A runner eats bread made from wheat and later uses that food energy to run. Which sequence correctly traces the energy?
options: Sunlight → glucose made in wheat chloroplasts → ATP made in the runner's mitochondria → movement and heat
Sunlight → ATP made in wheat mitochondria → glucose made in the runner's chloroplasts → movement and heat
Sunlight → glucose made in wheat chloroplasts → movement and heat → ATP made in the runner's mitochondria
Sunlight → oxygen made in wheat chloroplasts → energy stored in the runner's nucleus → movement and heat
why: Humans have no chloroplasts, and chloroplasts, not mitochondria, capture sunlight. The two organelles are swapped.
Movement is powered by ATP, so ATP must come before movement, not after it.
Oxygen does not carry the food energy; glucose does. And the nucleus holds DNA; it does not store energy for movement.
items.explain: The wheat's chloroplasts capture sunlight and store it as chemical energy in glucose (in the bread's starch). The runner's mitochondria release that energy into ATP, which powers movement, with some energy lost as heat. Energy flows one way through this chain.

items.prompt: Which two factors did the student keep the same so that light color was the only thing that changed? Select two answers.
options: The brightness of each lamp
The temperature of the water
The color of each filter
The volume of oxygen collected
How much green light chlorophyll reflects
why: Filter color is what the student changed on purpose. It is the independent variable.
The oxygen volume is what she measured. It is the dependent variable and was expected to change.
This is a property of chlorophyll given as background. It is not something the student set up or kept the same.
items.explain: The student kept lamp brightness (and distance) and water temperature (24 °C) the same; these are controlled variables. She also used the same amount of baking soda and the same kind of plant. Light color was the independent variable, and oxygen volume was the dependent variable.

items.prompt: Which discovery would contradict the cell theory?
options: A living thing that is not made of any cells
A living bacterium whose cell has no nucleus
A single cell that carries out all life processes
A new skin cell made when an old one divides
why: The cell theory does not require a nucleus. Bacteria have no nucleus and are alive, which fits the theory.
This fits the theory: the cell is the basic unit of life, and one cell can be a whole organism.
This fits the third part of the theory: cells come from existing cells.
items.explain: The first part of the cell theory says all living things are made of one or more cells. A living thing made of no cells would contradict it. The other three choices all agree with the theory.

items.prompt: A poison stops the mitochondria from working in a person's muscle cells. Which job will the muscle cells most directly be unable to do?
options: Release energy from glucose as ATP
Make glucose using energy from light
Build proteins from instructions in DNA
Control what enters and leaves the cell
why: Making glucose from light is photosynthesis, which happens in chloroplasts. Human cells have no chloroplasts.
Ribosomes build proteins. Mitochondria do not.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell, not the mitochondria.
items.explain: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration: they release energy from glucose and store it in ATP. Without working mitochondria, muscle cells cannot get the ATP they need to contract. This is how some poisons, such as cyanide, kill so quickly.

items.prompt:
Complete the sentences.

The outer boundary of an animal cell is its {{0}}. A bacterium differs from a plant cell because the bacterium has no {{1}}. In a plant cell, light energy is captured by the {{2}}.

options: cell membrane
cell wall
nucleus
vacuole
why: Animal cells have no cell wall. Their outer boundary is the flexible membrane.
The nucleus is inside the cell; it holds the DNA.
A vacuole is a storage sac inside the cell, not its boundary.

options: nucleus
cell wall
ribosomes
DNA
why: Most bacteria do have cell walls, just as plant cells do.
Every cell, including bacteria, has ribosomes to build proteins.
Bacteria do have DNA; it floats in the cytoplasm instead of sitting inside a nucleus.

options: chloroplasts
mitochondria
cell wall
ribosomes
why: Mitochondria release energy from glucose; they do not capture light.
The cell wall gives support and does not capture light.
Ribosomes build proteins and do not capture light.

items.explain: An animal cell's boundary is its cell membrane; it has no wall. Bacteria are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus, though they do have DNA, ribosomes, and usually a cell wall. Light energy is captured by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.

items.prompt:
C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

According to the equation, which substances does a cell release during cellular respiration, along with energy?
options: Carbon dioxide and water
Glucose and oxygen
Oxygen and water
Glucose and carbon dioxide
why: Glucose and oxygen are on the left side of the arrow. They are used up, not released.
Water is released, but oxygen is used up. You mixed a product with a reactant.
Carbon dioxide is released, but glucose is the fuel that is used up.
items.explain: Substances released are the products, on the right of the arrow: 6CO2 + 6H2O, so carbon dioxide and water, along with energy stored as ATP. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants on the left.

items.prompt: What is the mean volume of oxygen, in mL, used by the crickets at 30 °C? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 7.8 is the sum of the three trials. Divide by the number of trials: 7.8 ÷ 3 = 2.6.
2.5 is the middle value (the median), not the mean. Add all three trials and divide by 3.
You divided by 4, the number of rows in the table. There are three trials at 30 °C, so divide 7.8 by 3.

items.explain:
Trials at 30 °C: 2.5, 2.4, and 2.9 mL.

2.5 + 2.4 + 2.9 = 7.8

7.8 ÷ 3 = 2.6 mL

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: The crickets used oxygen faster as the temperature rose from 10 °C to 30 °C.
The crickets stop carrying out cellular respiration at temperatures below 10 °C.
The crickets gave off more oxygen into the chamber at higher temperatures.
Every kind of animal uses more oxygen when the air around it is warmer.
why: No temperature below 10 °C was tested, and at 10 °C the crickets still used 0.8 mL. The data cannot show respiration stopping.
The sensor measured oxygen used up, not given off. Animals use oxygen in respiration; they do not release it.
Only crickets were tested. Animals that keep a steady body temperature, such as people, may respond differently.
items.explain: Mean oxygen used: 0.8 mL at 10 °C, 1.6 mL at 20 °C, and 2.6 mL at 30 °C. Oxygen is a reactant of cellular respiration, so the crickets respired faster as temperature rose across the tested range. The empty chamber used 0.0 mL, so the change came from the crickets. Claims about other temperatures or every kind of animal go beyond the data.

items.prompt: A cow eats grass and later uses that food energy to walk. Which sequence correctly traces the energy?
options: Sunlight → glucose made in grass chloroplasts → ATP made in the cow's mitochondria → movement and heat
Sunlight → ATP made in grass mitochondria → glucose made in the cow's chloroplasts → movement and heat
Sunlight → glucose made in grass chloroplasts → movement and heat → ATP made in the cow's mitochondria
Sunlight → oxygen made in grass chloroplasts → energy stored in the cow's nucleus → movement and heat
why: Cows have no chloroplasts, and it is chloroplasts, not mitochondria, that capture sunlight. The two organelles are swapped.
Movement is powered by ATP, so ATP must come before movement, not after it.
Oxygen does not carry the food energy; glucose does. And the nucleus holds DNA; it does not store energy for movement.
items.explain: The grass's chloroplasts capture sunlight and store it in glucose. The cow eats the grass, and its mitochondria release that energy into ATP, which powers movement, with some lost as heat.

items.prompt: Which two factors did the student keep the same so that temperature was the only thing that changed? Select two answers.
options: The number of crickets in each trial
The length of time oxygen use was measured
The temperature of the chamber
The volume of oxygen the crickets used
Whether crickets match their surroundings
why: Temperature is what the student changed on purpose. It is the independent variable.
Oxygen used is what she measured. It is the dependent variable and was expected to change.
This is background about crickets. It is not something the student set up or held constant.
items.explain: The student used 10 crickets of the same size in every trial and measured oxygen use for the same 10 minutes each time; these are controlled variables. Temperature was the independent variable, and oxygen used was the dependent variable.

vocab.def: The smallest unit that can carry out all the processes of life.
vocab.example: A red blood cell, a single bacterium, a leaf cell

vocab.def: The scientific idea that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from existing cells.
vocab.example: A new skin cell forms when an existing skin cell divides.

vocab.def: A simple cell with no nucleus; its DNA floats in the cytoplasm.
A cell with a nucleus and organelles surrounded by membranes.
A small structure inside a cell that has a specific job.
The organelle that holds a cell's DNA and controls its activities.
vocab.example: The nucleus holds the instructions for making proteins.

vocab.def: The thin, flexible boundary around every cell that controls what goes in and out.
vocab.example: Oxygen passes through the cell membrane into the cell.

vocab.def: A stiff layer outside the cell membrane that supports and protects plant, fungus, and most bacterial cells.
vocab.example: Cell walls help a celery stalk stay firm.

vocab.def: The organelle where cellular respiration releases energy from glucose.
The green organelle in plants and algae where photosynthesis takes place.
vocab.example: Leaf cells are packed with chloroplasts.

vocab.def: The process in which plants and algae use light energy, carbon dioxide, and water to make glucose and release oxygen.
The process in which cells use oxygen to break down glucose and release energy, carbon dioxide, and water.
The molecule cells use to store and spend energy; often called the cell's energy currency.
vocab.example: Muscle cells use ATP to contract.

vocab.def: A way some cells release a small amount of energy from glucose without oxygen.
vocab.example: Yeast ferment sugar and release carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise.

vocab.def: Reactants are the substances that go into a chemical reaction (left of the arrow); products are the substances that come out (right of the arrow).
vocab.example: In photosynthesis, oxygen is a product.

notes:
Study Notes: Cells and Energy

Cell Theory

  1. All living things are made of cells.
  2. The cell is the basic unit of life.
  3. All cells come from existing cells.

Cell Types

Prokaryote (bacteria): no nucleus.
Eukaryote (plants, animals, fungi): nucleus + organelles.

Plant Only

Cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole.

Both Plant and Animal

Membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, mitochondria.

Organelle Jobs

  • Nucleus: holds DNA, controls cell
  • Membrane: controls what enters/leaves
  • Ribosome: makes proteins
  • Mitochondrion: respiration, ATP
  • Chloroplast: photosynthesis
  • Vacuole: storage
  • Cell wall: support
PhotosynthesisCellular Respiration
Equation6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)
WhereChloroplastsMitochondria
WhoPlants, algae, some bacteriaNearly all living things, including plants
WhenOnly in lightAll the time
EnergyStores light energy in glucoseReleases energy from glucose as ATP + heat

Energy flow: sunlight → glucose → ATP → work + heat. Without oxygen: fermentation (2 ATP per glucose; yeast make CO2 + alcohol, muscles make lactic acid).

Mystery cell: nucleus first (none = bacterium), then wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole (any = plant; none = animal). Not every plant cell is green: roots and bulbs lack chloroplasts.

Equation questions: list IN (left) and OUT (right) before reading the choices. Atoms = coefficient × subscript.

Indicator (BTB): yellow = more CO2 (respiration winning); blue = less CO2 (photosynthesis winning). In the dark, only respiration.
